To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the engineer's managerial prospects depend on the way his profession is perceived by the organisation and that the engineer's ability to survive a declining strategic importance of his profession depends on the development of generalist rather than specialist abilities.

the engineer's managerial prospects depend on the way the company's management defines the engineer's profession and that the engineer's power depends on the ability to develop generalist abilities rather that specialist ones.

the status of engineers in a company is determined by how the profession is defined by the organization, and that engineers are able to survive in a company when they develop generalist rather than specialist abilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way the engineer's work roles are perceived.
the relationship between occupational groups, the organisation and its environment.
the way the engineer's status is determined in the company, the factors which affect this status and the consequences of status for the engineer's work role and managerial prospects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the engineer is perceived as a manager, but not as a manager in a managerial position.
the engineer is perceived to be a manager.

engineering status is determined by a complex interaction of the engineer's qualifications and the company's definition of the profession, and by the ability of engineers to survive in a changing company.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
engineers are perceived as managers because they possess the necessary qualifications.
the engineer is perceived as a generalist, not a specialist; a manager, not a technician.
the engineering profession is in a state of flux and that the future of engineering in industry will depend on how engineers respond to the challenges of the 1990s.
The main takeaway from our work is that
engineers’ status as potential managers depends on how the company defines the engineering profession.
engineers’ power in organisations is not determined by their technical expertise, but rather their ability to develop generalist skills.
engineers are not necessarily managers.
